Md Shah Alam, Advocate (appearing in person)  ----- The Petitioner. 
None Appears ----- For the Opposite Parties

Shah Alam (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Abdul Hashem Bepari and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 8-6-98 passed by the District Judge, Bhola in Title Appeal No. 86 of 1990 reversing the judgment and decree dated 30-6-90 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Bhola in Title Suit No. 78 of 1986 decreeing the suit. 

 7. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the material evidence an record was pleased by the impugned judgment dated 30-6-90 to decree the suit on contest. 

 8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgment and decree contesting defendant No. 1 took an appeal before the District Judge, Bhola being Title Appeal No. 86 of 1990 and the learned District Judge by his impugned judgment dated 8-6-98 reversed the judgment of the trial Court and gave a money decree to the plaintiff for Taka 50,000 with simple interest @ 10% per annum from the date of bainapatra till realisation. 

 10. Mr Md Shah Alam, the learned Advocate appearing in person. submits that both the learned Courts below after having concurrently found that the contract in question is a genuine and valid one and the contesting defendant never pleading any case of hardship in his written statement, the learned District Judge evidently erred in law in giving the plaintiff a decree for money instead of a decree for specific performance of the contract by making out third case and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that in the absence of any pleading for hardship by stating even one word about it in the written statement as well as in the additional written statement and in the absence of any reliable evidence on record to prove any hardship for the contesting defendant in performing his part of the contract, the learned District Judge evidently erred in law in passing the impugned judgment ignoring the rules of pleadings and on illegal and irrelevant considerations and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the proved fact that he paid to defendant No.1 Taka 50,000 as back as in 1983 and the latter enjoyed full benefit of the money, the value of money has fallen many times in the course of the last 17 years, it is shockingly unjust and equitable to deprive the plaintiff of the benefit of the bargain and to let him off with his principal money with simple interest at the rate of 10% per annum in the name of solatium and the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 12.	The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has placed before me the plaint, the written statements as well as the impugned judgments. It appears that in the original written statement contesting defendant No. 1 denied the transaction as a whole and branded it as false and frivolous. But when the plaintiff, on the order of the Court. deposited necessary money as cost for examination and comparison of the admitted signatures of defendant No. 1 with his signatures appearing in the disputed bainapatra dated 30-11- 83, the contesting defendant realised his difficulty in sustaining his original stand and sought to avoid the opinion of the hand-writing expert by filing an additional written statement to state that he had earlier entered into a contract with one Ahmed Ali and in that connection he gave to Ahmed Ali some blank stamp papers containing his signatures but the said deed eventually did not materialise and the said signed blank papers remained with Ahmed Ali and it is possible that the plaintiff on obtaining the said stamp papers from Ahmed Ali has created the disputed bainapatra for making illegal gains. The signatures of defendant No. 1 in bainapatra dated 30-3-83, marked Exhibit 1, is thus an admitted fact. The contesting defendant had not the courage to deny his signature in Exhibit 1. The learned Subordinate Judge on detailed discussion and proper consideration of the evidence on record found that the disputed bainapatra Exhibit] is a genuine and valid one and on such finding decreed the suit in full. 

 13. On appeal, the learned District Judge also found the disputed bainapatra as a valid and genuine one but by making out a third case of hardship on the part of the contesting defendant in performing his part of the contract, refused a decree for specific performance of the contract. The precise reason for refusing a decree for specific performance of the contract by the learned District Judge appears to be the existence of structures standing in a portion of the suit land measuring one acre of land. 

 27. On consideration of the material evidence discussed above, the learned Courts below concurrently found that the disputed bainapatra dated 30-11-83, marked Exhibit 1 is a genuine and valid one. Although the learned trial Court clearly found that since no case of hardship was even pleaded by the contesting defendant in his written statement and his additional written statement and no case of real hardship could he made out at the trial, the plaintiff was entitled in law to get the solemn contract specifically enforced. The learned Court of appeal below on consideration of the evidence on record also found that the agreement for sale dated 30-11-83 as evidenced by Exhibit 1 is a genuine document. Both the learned Courts below also concurrently found that the contesting defendant had duly received from the plaintiff Taka 50000 as earnest money on 30-11-93. The learned Court of appeal after having recorded such a finding, however, refused a decree for the specific performance of the contract on the ground of hardship on the part of the contesting defendant, by making out a third case. 

 28. There is no dispute to the proposition of law that a decree for specific performance of a contract is essentially a matter of discretion for the Court but this discretion must be exercised according to sound judicial principles and not arbitrarily. It is equally settled that a contract duly entered into by the contracting parties has a solemnity of its own and ordinarily the Court has no option to refuse its specific performance unless it comes within the purview of an exception giving the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendant, or its performance would involve some hardship on the defendant which he did not foresee as an exception to the general rule as in section 22 of the SR Act. 

 30. It is of course, true that from the cross- examination of PWs 1-4 it has transpired that there exists a hut in the suit land where the defendant resides with the permission of the plaintiff. DW 1 and his witnesses stated about 2 huts and 2 ponds. There is overwhelming evidence on record to prove that the defendant owns about 3 acres of land in the vicinity of the suit property, a running shop at Borhanuddin Bazar, 3½ kathas of land at Tongi Bazar and a plot of land in Dhaka City. There is absolutely nothing or record to show that the defendant has no other place to reside other than the small hut standing in a comer of that suit property and he will be landing in extreme hardships if he is dislodged from that hut rendering him a destitute, a position which he could not foresee at the time of the contract. From the evidence on record, it is found that the defendant is a man of easy circumstances having a pretty good amount of agricultural and non-agricultural land and running shop at an upazila town. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, I am satisfied that the defendant has totally failed to make out any case of hardship to be entitled to the benefit of section 22 of the SR Act to avoid the solemn contract duly entered into by him with the plaintiff as back as on 30-11-83 and duly received Taka 50000 from the plaintiff as an earnest money and utilised the said money to the fullest possible extent deriving all the benefits out of the bargain. The plaintiff duly paid Taka 50000 to the defendant about 17 years ago in his humble bid to purchase the suit land. The value of money has undoubtedly fallen many times by now. If the plaintiff is now told on his face that instead of getting a decree for specific performance of the contract he will now be given a money decree, for no fault of his own, and no case of exception having been made out by the defendant, a great injustice would be perpetrated on the plaintiff which clearly stands out against equity, justice and good conscience. The injury to be sustained by the plaintiff will, indeed, far outweigh that of the defendant. 

 33. In reaching the ultimate conclusion in the case, I think, we should consider the age old maxim that "he who seeks equity must do equity himself." In this case, the defendant admittedly made no case of hardships in his pleadings and no case of real hardship has been made out at the trial. We are, therefore, required to consider the question of hardship to be suffered by the plaintiff out of the refusal of a decree for specific performance of the contract. The plaintiff has already deposited in the Court the balance of the consideration money amounting to Taka 10,000 only. I do not find any negligence on the part of the plaintiff to perform his part of the contract at any point of time but it is the defendant who sought to avoid a solemn contract by taking a false plea. In such circumstances, there can be no reason as to why the plaintiff should not be entitled to get a decree for specific performance of the contract as granted by the learned trial Court. I, therefore, find that the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in decreeing the suit for specific performance of the contract and the learned District Judge; Bhola seriously erred in law in refusing it on wholly illegal and irrelevant considerations, occasioning failure of justice. 

 34. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost and the impugned judgment and decree dated 6-8-98 passed by the learned District Judge, Bhola in Title Appeal No. 86 of 1990 are set aside and the judgment and decree dated 30-6-90 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola in Title Suit No. 78 of 1986 are restored. The plaintiff’s suit for specific performance of the contract stands decreed. Contesting defendant No. 1 is hereby directed to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property within 60 days of the receipt of the case records by the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola and to remove at his cost the hut standing in a comer of the suit property within the aforesaid time, failing which the plaintiff shall be at liberty to get the decree executed through the Court in accordance with law.
